results.subagent: Subagent D — Runtime Persistence and Recovery

findings.claim: There is NO SQLite/WAL or any embedded transactional database in the Octon runtime. The only 'sqlite' references (lifecycle_executor/src/codex.rs:47, kernel/src/lifecycle_program.rs:36030) are read-only references to the third-party Codex CLI's own '.codex/state_5.sqlite'. No Cargo.toml or Cargo.lock under .octon/framework declares rusqlite/sqlx/sled/rocksdb/redb/lmdb. The authoritative runtime state substrate is loose YAML + NDJSON files under .octon/state/{control,evidence,continuity}/. FD-005's mandated single local SQLite/WAL authoritative store does not exist.
findings.consequence: Grants, operations, evidence outbox, revocation, reconciliation and recovery cannot share a single atomic transaction boundary. Cross-record invariants (e.g. consume-token AND record-attempt AND reserve-capacity as one unit) are impossible; every multi-file mutation is a non-atomic sequence with partial-failure windows. Crash between two file writes leaves inconsistent state with no journal to roll forward/back atomically.
findings.minimum_repair: Introduce one embedded transactional store (rusqlite with WAL, or an equivalent single-writer log-structured store) as the authoritative substrate for grant/operation/token/revocation/reservation records, keeping the existing NDJSON run-journal as a derived export. Route all consequential state transitions through a single BEGIN/COMMIT.
findings.acceptance_test: grep for a DB dependency in .octon/framework/**/Cargo.toml returns a transactional store; a kill-point test that SIGKILLs the process between the token-consume write and the attempt-record write, on restart, shows either both records present or neither (no torn intermediate).

findings.claim: The single-use ('one-shot') effect-token consume in verify_authorized_effect is a read-check-write with a TOCTOU window and no lock. The record is loaded at effects.rs:294 (load_token_record), the guard 'if record.single_use && record.status == "consumed"' is checked at effects.rs:564, and the mutated record is written back at effects.rs:658 (persist_token_record). No file lock, advisory lock, or O_EXCL rename-based CAS is held across the load->check->write window. persist_token_record -> write_json (policy.rs:81-88) is a plain fs::write (no temp+rename, no fsync).
findings.consequence: Two concurrent verify_authorized_effect calls for the same single-use token can both pass the 'consumed' check before either writes 'consumed', double-consuming a one-shot grant (double dispatch of a consequential effect). Additionally, a crash mid-write of the token record (non-atomic fs::write) can truncate/corrupt the record JSON, making the token neither cleanly consumed nor re-consumable (load_token_record parse failure -> CapabilityDenied), i.e. a torn one-shot with no recovery path.
findings.minimum_repair: Make consume atomic: perform the consumed-status flip via a compare-and-swap (either a transactional UPDATE ... WHERE status<>'consumed' in the FD-005 store, or an O_EXCL 'consumed marker' file created before the effect that fails the second caller). Write the token record via temp+fsync+rename. Hold the guard and the write inside one critical section.
findings.acceptance_test: Adversarial test: spawn N concurrent verify_authorized_effect calls against one single_use token; assert exactly one returns VerifiedEffect and N-1 return EFFECT_TOKEN_ALREADY_CONSUMED. Kill-point test: SIGKILL during persist_token_record and confirm the record is either fully old or fully 'consumed', never truncated.

findings.claim: The entire authority_engine writes state non-atomically. authority_engine/src has 11 non-test fs::write call sites and ZERO sync_all/atomic-rename usage. Grant bundles (authority.rs:412 write_authority_grant_bundle -> write_yaml -> fs::write at policy.rs:95), token records, decision artifacts, and token-consumption receipts are all written with plain fs::write. Atomic temp+fsync+rename helpers DO exist but only in isolated spots: kernel/src/scaffold.rs:298 (atomic_write), wasm_host/src/scoped_fs.rs:539 (atomic_write_file, incl. fsync_dir_best_effort), wasm_host/src/kv_store.rs:100, and a partial temp+rename (no fsync) in kernel/src/lifecycle_run_admission.rs:458 publish_artifact_set.
findings.consequence: A crash during any authority-engine state write (grant bundle, decision artifact, token record, revocation) can leave a truncated/half-written YAML/JSON file. On restart the file fails to parse and the run is either wedged (CapabilityDenied) or, worse, a partially-written grant could be re-read as valid. Durability is not guaranteed even for cleanly-written files (no fsync) so a power loss can lose acknowledged state.
findings.minimum_repair: Provide one shared atomic_write(path, bytes) helper (temp in same dir + write_all + sync_all + rename + best-effort dir fsync) in core and route ALL authority_engine/core state writes (write_json/write_yaml) through it; or fold these records into the FD-005 transactional store.
findings.acceptance_test: Static: grep authority_engine/src for fs::write returns zero call sites that bypass an atomic helper. Kill-point: SIGKILL during write_authority_grant_bundle; on restart the grant file is either the full previous version or the full new version, and always parses.

findings.claim: There is no reservation / capacity-reservation-in-the-same-transaction mechanism, and there IS a standalone lease subsystem (the exact anti-pattern FD-013 forbids). Route-write-leases are written to their own .octon/state/evidence/.../route-write-leases/*.yml files via naive fs::write (lifecycle_program.rs:10947-10955), explicitly self-described as 'dispatch-preflight-only' (line 10931-10933) and 'does not authorize mutation' (10928-10930). token_budget.rs is a write-out ledger (write_route_token_budget_ledger at line 134) with no reserve/decrement/remaining logic. Nothing reserves evidence capacity atomically with the operation record; there is no evidence 'outbox' at all (grep for outbox/capacity_reservation across framework+instance returns nothing).
findings.consequence: Capacity/budget can be exceeded under crash or concurrency because it is tracked in a separate ledger file written after (or independent of) the operation, not reserved in the same commit. The standalone route-write-lease files can drift from the operation records they gate (lease says bound while the operation never happened, or vice versa) with no transactional link. FD-013's requirement that evidence-capacity be reserved in the same transaction and that there be NO standalone lease subsystem is directly violated.
findings.minimum_repair: Fold capacity reservation into the same transaction as the operation-attempt record in the FD-005 store (reserve N units and insert the attempt row atomically; release on terminal outcome). Retire route-write-lease *.yml as a standalone durable authority; if retained, make it a derived read-only projection of the transactional reservation, not an independent file.
findings.acceptance_test: Static: no code path reserves capacity in a file/table distinct from the operation record's transaction. Concurrency test: two operations each requesting > half of a capacity budget cannot both succeed. Crash test: SIGKILL after reservation but before operation commit leaves zero net reserved capacity on restart.

findings.claim: There is no unknown-outcome / uncertain-external-effect reconciliation engine. For consequential external effects (git push/publication), the actual mutation is delegated to the agent/executor and is NOT re-verified post-hoc: grep across kernel for post-push confirmation (ls-remote / rev-parse against remote after push) finds only validation predicates that assert push MUST NOT have happened (lifecycle_program.rs:19499, 19518 forbidden-actions lists) — never a path that, after attempting a push, reconciles whether it actually landed. The only 'recovery' surface is passive status fields (orchestration.rs:140 recovery_status / recovery_reason, and lease_expires_at/last_heartbeat_at in the run-status YAML) plus an O_EXCL child lock (lifecycle_program.rs:24991 acquire_child_lock) with stale-lock detection. replay_store (replay_store/src/lib.rs) reconstructs state from a hash-chained journal and gates live side-effect replay, but it operates only on already-recorded events; it does not resolve 'did the push land?' for an in-flight attempt whose process died.
findings.consequence: If the runtime crashes after dispatching a consequential external effect (e.g. git push) but before the terminal outcome is durably recorded, on restart the system cannot determine whether the effect landed. There is no attempt->pending->{committed|failed}->reconciled state machine for external effects, so recovery either blindly retries (risking duplicate side effect) or blocks a human. FD-012's unknown-outcome handling, reconciliation, and terminal-state requirements are not implemented as a runtime mechanism.
findings.minimum_repair: Add an attempt lifecycle to the FD-005 store: record intent (pending) before the external call, record outcome (committed/failed) after; on restart, for each pending attempt, run an idempotent reconcile probe (e.g. git ls-remote to check whether the ref landed) to reach a terminal state before any retry. Make retries keyed by the attempt idempotency_key.
findings.acceptance_test: Kill-point test: SIGKILL immediately after a git push subprocess returns but before the terminal record is written; on restart the reconcile path queries the remote, classifies the attempt as committed-observed or failed, and does NOT re-push a landed ref. A pending attempt is never left with no terminal state after reconcile runs.

findings.claim: Attempt-state and idempotency exist only partially and non-transactionally. The run-journal (replay_store RunJournalEvent) carries an optional idempotency_key field (replay_store/src/lib.rs:171) and hash-chains events; lifecycle requests carry retry_attempt (lifecycle_executor/src/request.rs:100) and terminal executor states 'completed-observed'/'timed-out' exist (observed in adapter behavior). But idempotency_key is Option and not enforced as a uniqueness/dedup key against a store (no unique-index / no dedup lookup on replay of an attempt), and there is no durable attempt row that is transactionally advanced through reservation->consume->outcome->terminal. Cross-process de-dup relies on the per-process in-memory Mutex<HashMap> 'inflight' (kernel/src/stdio.rs:98) which does not survive a crash and does not coordinate across processes.
findings.consequence: Idempotency is advisory (a field in a journal event), not enforced by a store that rejects a duplicate attempt. After a crash the in-memory inflight guard is gone, so a re-dispatched attempt with the same logical identity is not automatically deduplicated at the persistence layer, permitting duplicate consequential effects. FD-012's requirement that every consequential effect carry enforced idempotency and a single terminal state per attempt is only partly met.
findings.minimum_repair: Make idempotency_key mandatory for consequential effects and enforce it with a unique constraint in the FD-005 store; on re-dispatch, look up the prior attempt and return its recorded terminal outcome instead of re-executing. Persist attempt state (not just an in-memory map) so it survives restart.
findings.acceptance_test: Submit the same consequential effect twice with the same idempotency_key across two separate process invocations; assert the second is short-circuited to the first attempt's terminal outcome and the external side effect executes exactly once.

decision_alignment.rationale: FD-005 mandates one local SQLite/WAL authoritative store spanning grants, operations, evidence outbox, revocation, reconciliation and recovery. The repository has NO embedded transactional DB at all (no rusqlite/sqlx/sled/redb/lmdb in any framework Cargo.toml or Cargo.lock; the only sqlite refs are to the third-party Codex CLI's own state file). The authoritative substrate is loose YAML+NDJSON files under .octon/state/{control,evidence,continuity}, written largely via non-atomic fs::write with zero fsync in the authority engine. There is no shared transaction boundary, no outbox, and no single-store recovery. This is the opposite of what FD-005 requires.

Several FD-012 primitives exist in skeletal form: a single_use one-shot consume (effects.rs:564), retry_attempt counter, terminal executor states (completed-observed/timed-out), an optional idempotency_key in the run-journal, and a hash-chained journal + replay planner. But none are transactional or crash-safe: the one-shot consume is a lockless read-check-write TOCTOU (effects.rs:294->564->658) persisted non-atomically; idempotency is advisory (Option field, no enforced uniqueness/dedup store); cross-process de-dup relies on a per-process in-memory Mutex that dies on crash (stdio.rs:98); there is NO reservation, NO evidence outbox, and NO unknown-outcome reconciliation engine for uncertain external effects (e.g. did a git push land). Reservation/consume/attempt/idempotency/unknown-outcome/reconciliation/terminal-state are not implemented as one atomic per-effect lifecycle.

FD-013 requires evidence-capacity to be reserved in the SAME transaction as the operation and forbids a standalone lease subsystem. The repo does the opposite: capacity/budget is tracked in a separate write-out token-budget-ledger with no reserve/decrement semantics (token_budget.rs), and there IS a standalone route-write-lease subsystem writing independent .octon/state/.../route-write-leases/*.yml files via naive fs::write (lifecycle_program.rs:10947-10955), explicitly 'dispatch-preflight-only' and not transactionally linked to the operation it gates. No transaction reserves evidence capacity together with the operation; there is no evidence outbox.
evidence: grep across .octon/framework + .octon/instance for outbox/capacity_reservation returns nothing

strengths_to_preserve: replay_store crate (replay_store/src/lib.rs) provides a genuinely useful hash-chained run-journal model: per-event previous_event_hash chaining, validate_journal sequence+hash-drift detection (line 554), reconstruct_runtime_state, and a replay planner that fail-closed denies live side-effecting replay without FreshReplayAuthorization (line 776-797). This is a strong journal/audit primitive to keep as the DERIVED export layer on top of a future transactional store.

The single_use effect-token model in authority_engine/effects.rs (record.single_use + status='consumed' + EFFECT_TOKEN_ALREADY_CONSUMED rejection) is the right shape for one-shot consume; it needs a transactional CAS underneath, not a redesign.

The consumption pipeline already records a request event BEFORE mutation and a consumed event, plus a consumption receipt (effects.rs:576-647) — a good intent-before-effect ordering that a proper attempt lifecycle can build on.

Atomic write helpers already exist and are correct where used: kernel/src/scaffold.rs:298 atomic_write (temp+sync_all+rename) and wasm_host/src/scoped_fs.rs:539 atomic_write_file (temp+sync_all+rename+dir fsync). These should be promoted to a shared core helper and used everywhere.

publish_artifact_set (lifecycle_run_admission.rs:458) already refuses to overwrite canonical artifacts and stages+renames as a set with rollback of partial publishes — a create-once discipline worth keeping (needs fsync added).

The run-status model already carries recovery_status/recovery_reason/lease_expires_at/last_heartbeat_at fields (orchestration.rs:140), giving a schema hook for a real recovery/reconcile engine to populate.
uncertainties: I did not run any process, kill-point, or concurrency test (READ-ONLY constraint). The TOCTOU double-consume (D-02), torn-write corruption (D-03), and unknown-outcome gaps (D-05) are STATICALLY_INSPECTED architectural inferences from the code paths; proving them exploitable requires the REQUIRES_DYNAMIC_PROOF acceptance tests I specified.

I did not exhaustively read all ~98k LOC of the kernel crate; there may be a reservation or reconciliation path in a kernel command I did not open (I grepped for reserve/capacity/reconcile/outbox/unknown-outcome across the whole workspace and found only what is cited). If such a path exists it is not discoverable by the standard vocabulary and is not wired into the authority-engine consume path I traced.

Whether verify_authorized_effect (and thus the one-shot consume) is on the ACTUAL git-push/publication dispatch path is only partially confirmed: I confirmed it is called for stdio service invocations (stdio.rs:344) and in execution.rs/workflow.rs, but per prior repo knowledge the executor's real git mutations are agent-delegated and may bypass it. The mediation-gap question is Subagent-scope-adjacent; I flag it because it determines whether FD-012's one-shot guarantee is enforceable at the effect boundary at all.

I treated the intake handoff unit as research-only and did not rely on it. FD text was taken from the assignment summary, not from a canonical decision file I read; if the canonical FD-005/012/013 wording differs (e.g. permits a non-SQLite transactional store), FD-005's alignment could soften from CONTRADICTED to PARTIALLY_SATISFIED, but the absence of ANY transactional store keeps it at minimum ABSENT/CONTRADICTED.
fsync-of-directory semantics on macOS (the dev platform) differ from Linux; even the 'atomic' helpers' durability guarantees are platform-dependent and unverified at runtime.

results.subagent: Subagent E — Evidence, Attestation, Support Claims (FD-013, FD-014)

findings.claim: FD-014 mandates that broker/verifier 'sign' direct observations and that checkpoints be 'signed', but the runtime implements NO cryptographic signing of any kind: the only crypto dependency across all 13 crates is unkeyed SHA-256 (sha2) plus hex. There is no ed25519/hmac/ring/dalek/ecdsa crate, no keypair, no secret/signing key, and no signature field on any evidence, event, or checkpoint. Journal integrity is a plain unkeyed hash chain (replay_store digest_value = Sha256::digest(serde_json bytes); kernel program_event_hash = sha256_digest of the event with its hash field zeroed). Because the hash is unkeyed and the hashing algorithm is public code, any actor with write access to the retained event log can rewrite any event and deterministically recompute the entire downstream chain, producing a chain that passes validate_event_hash_chain / validate_journal. Hash chaining detects accidental corruption and naive single-event edits, NOT authenticated rewriting or non-repudiation.
findings.consequence: FD-014's required proof — 'Rechaining breaks checkpoint verification' — is FALSE as implemented. Rechaining does NOT break verification because nothing signs the chain head or checkpoint with a secret; the verifier only recomputes the same public hash the tamperer already recomputed. Support claims that lean on 'signed' evidence, non-repudiation, or unforgeable checkpoints are unsupported. The genuine tamper-evidence property comes only from the fact that event logs are git-tracked and pushed to GitHub (content-addressed commit history with a remote copy), not from any in-repo signing.
findings.minimum_repair: Either (a) implement real signing: add an ed25519 (or HMAC with an operator-held key) signature over each event-log head / checkpoint, sign at seal time with a key the writer holds, and verify the signature (not just recompute the hash) at closeout/promotion; or (b) if signing is intentionally out of scope for a solo local-first builder, amend FD-014 and all governance/schema wording to say 'hash-chained and git-anchored' instead of 'signed', and document that tamper-evidence relies on the external git/GitHub commit history rather than in-repo cryptographic signatures.
findings.acceptance_test: Take a retained events.ndjson for a closed run, edit a payload/effect field of a non-terminal event, recompute event_sha256 and all downstream previous_event_sha256 with the public program_event_hash algorithm, then run the closeout/promotion hash-chain validator. Under the current implementation the rechained log passes (demonstrating the gap). Under a correct fix, signature verification against the writer's key must fail on the rewritten head.

findings.claim: Neither RunCheckpointRecord (Rust) nor checkpoint-v2.schema.json (contract) carries any signature, MAC, or signed-head field. checkpoint-v2 declares mutable_state_digest and artifact_digests (SHA-256 digests) and run-event-v2 declares hash_algorithm const 'sha256' with previous_event_hash/event_hash — i.e. hash-chaining only. There is no 'signed checkpoint' concept anywhere in the framework, instance, or kernel code (grep for 'signed checkpoint'/'checkpoint signature' returns nothing).
findings.consequence: FD-014's 'signed checkpoints' are absent at both the code and contract layer. A checkpoint cannot 'detect retained-evidence rewriting' via signature because it has no signature field; it only references digests that a rewriter can recompute. PROOF-EVIDENCE ('Signed checkpoints detect retained-evidence rewriting') has no supporting primitive.
findings.minimum_repair: Add a signed-head field (e.g. checkpoint_signature over {run_id, checkpoint_id, event_position, last_event_hash, artifact_digests}) to checkpoint-v2.schema.json and RunCheckpointRecord, produced with an operator/broker key and verified on load; or downgrade the FD-014 language and schema comments to 'digest-anchored, git-tracked checkpoint' and state the detection boundary explicitly.
findings.acceptance_test: grep the checkpoint schema and RunCheckpointRecord struct for a signature/MAC field: today there is none. A correct fix adds a signature field whose verification is exercised by a test that rewrites the checkpointed artifacts and asserts verification fails.

findings.claim: The capability service layer emits 'attestations' whose 'signature' field is generated by hash_text() = plain unkeyed 'shasum -a 256' (falling back to 'sha256sum', and finally to 'cksum' — a CRC32 checksum) over the public string 'role|actor|plan_hash|evidence_hash|run_id'. Any party who knows those inputs can recompute the identical 'signature'. Worse, the policy_engine quorum check never verifies the signature value: it counts attestation entries whose signature string is merely non-empty (!value.trim().is_empty()) and checks that plan_hash/evidence_hash strings match — a literal signature of 'x' satisfies quorum.
findings.consequence: The proposer/verifier/recovery 'signatures' (ACP-2+ quorum) provide zero authenticity and zero non-repudiation, and are not even validated cryptographically — quorum is presence-counting theater. The field name 'signature' overstates the guarantee (support-claim inaccuracy). A single actor can fabricate all three attestations, or supply arbitrary non-empty strings, to clear the quorum gate.
findings.minimum_repair: Replace hash_text-based 'signature' with a real MAC/signature keyed to the attesting actor and verify it in the policy_engine quorum check (verify the signature over the bound plan_hash/evidence_hash, not just count non-empty strings and enforce distinct actor identities). If real signing is out of scope, rename the field (e.g. 'attestation_digest') and document that quorum enforces role/actor presence and hash-binding only, not cryptographic authenticity.
findings.acceptance_test: Construct an AcpRequest with three attestations all authored by the same actor and signature values of literal 'x' (or hash_text recomputed by any party): current policy_engine clears quorum (min_signatures satisfied, roles present). A correct fix rejects it for unverifiable/forged signatures and/or non-distinct attesters.

findings.claim: FD-013 requires reserving required evidence capacity in the same transaction as the operation, with the proof that near-full storage still records denial, failure, revocation, rollback, and closeout. No evidence-capacity reservation, disk/free-space check, ENOSPC handling, or storage-pressure concept exists anywhere in the runtime or governance (grep across all crates and .octon/framework|instance is empty). Evidence writes use plain fs::write (write_json/write_yaml) with no fsync/sync_all and no temp-file-then-rename atomicity, and the consequential-run evidence bundle spans many separate files written independently.
findings.consequence: FD-013's safety property is unproven: under near-full storage, an fs::write can produce a truncated/partial file or fail mid-bundle, leaving terminal evidence (denial/failure/revocation/rollback/closeout) missing or corrupt with no reservation guaranteeing space for those terminal records and no ordering/atomicity guarantee that they land. The behavioral-contract promise 'never lose recoverable work' (PROOF-CRASH-SAFETY) is not backstopped for the full-disk case.
findings.minimum_repair: Add a minimal capacity reservation or pre-flight free-space check that pre-allocates space for the mandatory terminal-evidence records before beginning a consequential operation, and make evidence writes atomic (write to a temp file, fsync, rename) so a mid-write failure never yields a partial canonical record; alternatively, prove via an fault-injection test that terminal-evidence writes are ordered-first and durable even when subsequent writes fail on a full volume.
findings.acceptance_test: Run a consequential lifecycle on a filesystem constrained to a few KB free (fault injection): assert denial/failure/revocation/rollback/closeout records are still written completely and pass validation, and that no canonical evidence file is left truncated. Current code has no mechanism ensuring this.

findings.claim: FD-013's negative constraint — 'no standalone lease subsystem/service' — is satisfied. The only 'lease' primitive in the runtime is the network-egress exception lease, a time-boxed governance INPUT file under .octon/state/control/execution/exceptions/leases/ that is evaluated inline by evaluate_network_egress (not a service or lifecycle). The journal field capability_lease_ref is an Option<String> governing-ref that is always None in the code paths inspected (telemetry_sink, replay_store defaults).
findings.consequence: This half of FD-013 is met: there is no separate capacity/capability lease service or lifecycle to maintain, consistent with the solo-builder simplicity rationale. The exception-lease mechanism is a policy input, not a lifecycle service, and should be preserved as-is.
findings.minimum_repair: None required for the negative constraint. Keep the inline exception-lease evaluation model.
findings.acceptance_test: grep the crates for any lease service/lifecycle/daemon: only the inline network-egress exception-lease evaluator exists. No standalone lease subsystem is instantiated.

findings.claim: Support-claim accuracy is generally HONEST for the completeness half of FD-014 but the 'signed' vocabulary is overstated. evidence-store-v1.md correctly uses 'hash-match' (not 'signed') for the journal mirror and states honest fail-closed completeness rules ('missing required evidence blocks closure, promotion, or live claim activation'; retained snapshot must hash-match the live control journal at closeout). The platform-overview doc calls ACP-2+ artifacts 'attestations' and 'signature' without qualifying that these are unkeyed recomputable hashes. No governance/spec doc claims 'tamper-proof', 'non-repudiation', or 'cryptographically signed' evidence (grep is empty), so the framework avoids the worst overclaims — but FD-014's own register text ('Broker and verifier sign direct observations; signed checkpoints') is the overclaim relative to the implementation.
findings.consequence: The 'honest completeness claims' clause of FD-014 is met by the evidence-store completeness rules and fail-closed hash-match requirement. The 'signed observations / signed checkpoints' clause is not met and its vocabulary overstates the actual guarantee. A reader trusting FD-014 as written would believe the system provides cryptographic non-repudiation it does not.
findings.minimum_repair: Reconcile the FD-014 register text and platform-overview attestation description with reality: replace 'sign'/'signed'/'signature' with 'hash-chain and git-anchor' (or implement real signing per E-01/E-03). Keep the evidence-store-v1 completeness/hash-match language unchanged — it is accurate.
findings.acceptance_test: Audit every governance use of 'sign(ed)/signature/attestation' against the implementation: each must either map to a verified cryptographic signature or be reworded to 'hash/digest/git-anchored'. The evidence-store completeness rules should already pass this audit; the FD-014 register text and ACP attestation docs should fail until reworded or backed by real signing.

findings.claim: The evidence-retention-contract-v1 schema exists but is a container of free-text string rule arrays (retention_rules/integrity_rules/retrieval_rules as arrays of prose strings), and no concrete active instance of it was found (only framework README/family references and log mentions). There is no machine-enforced bounded-retention or compaction routine that re-verifies the hash chain after compaction. The 'compact evidence views' (evidence-index, raw-log-summary, failing-slice-manifest, retained-run-evidence-index) are declared as non-authoritative aids that must fail closed on digest mismatch and must not overwrite raw evidence — but they are reduction/summary views, not a retention-bound compaction that preserves and re-anchors chain verifiability.
findings.consequence: FD-014's 'bounded retention, compaction' with the proof 'compaction preserves verifiability' is only partially represented: compact views preserve source digests and fail closed on mismatch (good), but there is no enforced retention bound or a compaction operation that re-establishes a verifiable (let alone signed) head over the compacted set. Operational evidence volume for a solo builder is bounded only by ad-hoc external-localization/cleanup helpers, not by an active retention policy instance.
findings.minimum_repair: Instantiate an active evidence-retention-contract with concrete bounded-retention limits, and define a compaction operation that, when it drops or archives raw events, retains a verifiable digest-anchored (ideally signed per E-01) checkpoint over the compacted range so post-compaction verification still detects rewriting; add a test that compacts a run and re-verifies chain integrity.
findings.acceptance_test: Compact a run's raw evidence per the retention policy, then run chain/checkpoint verification over the compacted bundle and assert it still detects a rewrite of a compacted-range artifact. Today no such compaction+re-verification path exists.

decision_alignment.rationale: The negative constraint ('no standalone lease subsystem') is SATISFIED: the only lease is an inline time-boxed network-egress exception-lease policy input, and capability_lease_ref is an unused optional journal ref — there is no lease service or lifecycle. However, the positive requirement — reserve required evidence capacity in the same transaction, with proof that near-full storage still records denial/failure/revocation/rollback/closeout — is ABSENT: no capacity reservation, no free-space/ENOSPC check, and non-atomic plain fs::write for evidence with no fsync or temp-rename. On a full disk the mandatory terminal evidence can be lost or truncated. Net: half satisfied (negative constraint), half absent (safety proof).
evidence: grep of all crates + .octon/framework|instance for capacity-reservation/ENOSPC/free-space: empty

decision_alignment.rationale: FD-014 says broker/verifier 'sign' direct observations and mandates 'signed checkpoints' whose required proof is 'rechaining breaks checkpoint verification'. The implementation performs NO cryptographic signing: the only crypto dependency is unkeyed SHA-256 (sha2)+hex; no ed25519/hmac/ring/dalek/ecdsa, no keypair, no signing key, and no signature field on any event, checkpoint, or evidence record. Integrity is an unkeyed, publicly recomputable hash chain (digest_value/program_event_hash), so an actor with write access can rewrite retained events and recompute a fully 'verified' chain — rechaining does NOT break verification. The service-layer 'attestation signatures' are hash_text (plain shasum, cksum fallback), never cryptographically verified (policy quorum merely counts non-empty signature strings). The honest-completeness half is met (evidence-store-v1 uses 'hash-match', fail-closed 'missing required evidence blocks closure'), and bounded-retention/compaction is only partially represented. But the core 'signed observations / signed checkpoints' requirement and its required proof are contradicted by the implementation; the real tamper-evidence anchor is git/GitHub commit history, not signing.
evidence: .octon/framework/engine/runtime/crates/policy_engine/src/lib.rs:2586-2614 (quorum counts non-empty signature strings, never verifies)
.octon/framework/engine/runtime/spec/evidence-store-v1.md:229-243,302-318 (honest hash-match + fail-closed completeness — the one clause that holds)

strengths_to_preserve: Unkeyed SHA-256 hash chaining IS a genuine primitive worth keeping: replay_store validate_journal and kernel validate_event_hash_chain reliably detect accidental corruption, sequence gaps, run-id mismatch, and naive single-event edits, and are deterministic/canonical (hash-field-zeroed serialization). It just must not be MARKETED as signing/non-repudiation.

Event logs (events.ndjson) are git-tracked (not gitignored) and pushed to GitHub, giving a real, content-addressed, remotely-replicated tamper-evidence anchor. This is the actual property FD-014 gets — worth naming explicitly as the trust root instead of claiming in-repo signing.

evidence-store-v1.md completeness rules are honest and fail-closed: 'missing required evidence blocks closure, promotion, or live claim activation'; the retained journal snapshot must hash-match the live control journal at closeout (lines 237, 310). This directly satisfies FD-014's 'honest completeness claims' clause and should be preserved verbatim.

Compact evidence views (evidence-index, raw-log-summary, failing-slice-manifest, retained-run-evidence-index) are correctly declared non-authoritative, carry source digests, and fail closed on digest mismatch without overwriting raw evidence — a sound reduction model for solo-builder context budgets.

FD-013's simplicity choice is honored in code: no standalone lease/capacity service exists; the inline network-egress exception-lease (time-boxed, state='active', expiry-checked) is a lightweight policy input rather than a subsystem. Keep this model.

Checkpoint and event schemas already carry digests (mutable_state_digest, artifact_digests, previous_event_hash, event_hash) — the structural slots to add a real signature/MAC over the head exist, so upgrading to true signing (if chosen) is an additive change, not a redesign.
uncertainties: I did not execute any test or run the runtime (READ-ONLY, no cargo). The claim that a rechained event log passes validation (E-01 acceptance test) is a static/architectural inference from reading program_event_hash + validate_event_hash_chain; it is very high-confidence but classified STATICALLY_INSPECTED, not DYNAMICALLY_EXECUTED.

I did not exhaustively enumerate every callsite of validate_event_hash_chain / validate_journal across the ~98k-LOC kernel; I confirmed the kernel uses its own validate_event_hash_chain (lifecycle_program.rs:7527, 21077) and that replay_store::validate_journal is not referenced outside replay_store, but there may be additional verification paths I did not trace. This does not change the signing conclusion (no signing primitive exists to call).

The FD-013/FD-014 decision text I relied on comes from the intake unit's final-decision-register.yml (RESEARCH INPUT, possibly stale). If the operator-accepted register maintained elsewhere differs, the exact wording ('sign'/'signed') I am testing against could differ — but the code facts (no signing crate/key/field) are independent of that.

I did not fully audit the OwnerAttestationConfig / require_quorum_token path (policy_engine.rs owner-attestation flow beyond line 2740) to confirm whether an owner attestation or quorum_token is ever cryptographically bound; the portions read show presence/role/hash-binding checks only, no signature verification, but a keyed quorum_token verification could exist deeper. If it does, E-03's severity for the owner path could be lower.

Whether disk-full atomicity is handled at a lower layer (e.g. OS/filesystem journaling, or a wrapper I did not find) is UNVERIFIED; I found no application-level reservation, fsync, or temp-rename in the inspected write helpers, but I did not audit every write path in kernel/side_effects exhaustively.

The evidence-retention-contract-v1 has no active instance in the paths I searched; it is possible an instance lives in a path I excluded (e.g. .octon/generated) or is produced at runtime. I classified FD-014's retention/compaction clause as PARTIALLY_SATISFIED on that basis with medium confidence.

results.subagent: Subagent F — Self-Development and Trust Root (FD-017, FD-018)

findings.claim: The self-evolution / promotion / recertification runtime (octon evolve, octon promote, octon recertify) is inspection-only and is not invoked by any merge/CI gate; it therefore does not enforce that trust-root or ordinary self-development changes actually pass through the evolution/promotion/recertification process before they take effect on main.
findings.consequence: The entire self-evolution control surface (candidate/classify/simulate/lab/propose/promote/recertify) is a hand-run CLI advisory. `apply_promotion` (evolution.rs:425-469) only reads state and returns `ready_to_apply`/`blocked` reports; it performs no file write and no activation. A grep of .github/workflows shows only uec-cutover-certify.yml references 'recertif' (a one-time UEC closure workflow, workflow_dispatch/push, not a merge gate), and NO workflow invokes `octon evolve`/`octon promote`/`octon recertify` or the octon-self-evolution program. Nothing mechanically forces a self-development change (ordinary Class-B-shaped or trust-root) to be classified, lab-gated, promotion-receipted, or recertified before it merges. The FD-017 discipline exists only as governance prose that an agent may bypass by editing files directly and merging via the normal Change routes.
findings.minimum_repair: Add a required merge gate (e.g. a new job in closure-certification.yml or a dedicated self-evolution-gate.yml) that, for any diff touching declared trust-root/authority surfaces, fails closed unless a matching promotion receipt + accepted self-evolution-decision-request + recertification-result exist and validate; wire `octon promote apply`/`octon recertify run` (or an equivalent validator) into that gate so the runtime that encodes the discipline is actually on the enforced path.
findings.acceptance_test: Create a branch that edits a trust-root file (e.g. .octon/framework/constitution/charter.yml) with no promotion receipt / decision request / recertification result and open a PR; the new required gate must fail closed. A second PR that includes a valid receipt+decision+recertification for that exact change must pass. Confirm the gate job appears in the branch ruleset required checks.

findings.claim: Merge/certification gates check out and run the PR's own head ref, so a change that edits its own gate workflow, its own validator script, or its own governing policy is certified by the edited (post-change) version — a same-change self-certification path with no independent verifier.
findings.consequence: closure-certification.yml runs `validate-promotion-receipts.sh`, `validate-authorization-boundary-coverage.sh`, `validate-generated-non-authority.sh`, etc. from the checked-out PR head (checkout at closure-certification.yml:40-41). harness-self-containment.yml likewise validates workflow/validator changes from the PR head (checkout:48-49) and its `paths:` list (lines 7-33) even scopes-in edits to the trust-root workflows themselves (main-change-route-guard.yml, main-push-safety.yml, release-please.yml, runtime-binaries.yml, harness-self-containment.yml). Because the verifier is inside the same change surface it gates, a PR can weaken or neutralize its own validator/gate/policy and be certified by the weakened version. This directly violates FD-017's 'cannot self-certify' clause and FD-018's 'candidate cannot change its own verification/activation/rollback rules'.
findings.minimum_repair: Pin the trust-root verifier set to a trusted ref: for gates that certify authority/trust-root surfaces, check out the verifier scripts and gate workflows from the base branch (or a signed/pinned tag) rather than the PR head, or run those gates via `pull_request_target` with an explicit checkout of `github.event.pull_request.base.sha` for the verifier while diffing the head; add a distinct required check that fails whenever a diff touches a verifier/gate file without an independent (base-ref) re-run and an operator approval.
findings.acceptance_test: Open a PR that edits `.octon/framework/assurance/runtime/_ops/scripts/validate-promotion-receipts.sh` to `exit 0` unconditionally AND removes a promotion receipt; under current code the closure-certification job passes. After the repair, the base-ref verifier must run and fail closed, and a separate required check must flag the verifier-file edit for independent approval.

findings.claim: There is no inert-landing mechanism for trust-root changes: authored authority under .octon/framework/** and .octon/instance/** (constitution, charter, policies, gate workflows, validators) takes effect the instant it lands on main; nothing lets a trust-root change land dormant and require a separate, later activation step.
findings.consequence: The only 'activation' concept (promotion-activation-v1.md:43-51, promotion-semantics.yml release_activation) is a documentation/receipt discipline for flipping the live *disclosure/release* claim (harness-card / release-lineage), and it is enforced by no runtime crate code (grep of crates/ for release_lineage/active_release/harness_card in runtime code returned nothing). Constitution/charter/policy/workflow/validator files are read live at HEAD by CI and by the runtime resolver, so a merged edit to any of them is immediately effective. There is no feature-flag/staging gate that holds a trust-root change dormant pending an independent activation decision. FD-017's 'trust-root changes land inert' is therefore ABSENT as an implemented control; the charter Amendment Policy (CHARTER.md:136-143) requires 'human governance approval' in the same branch but supplies no inert/two-phase landing.
findings.minimum_repair: Introduce a staged-activation primitive for trust-root surfaces: land trust-root changes into a non-effective staging location or behind an explicit effective-selector (e.g. a `state/control/**` activation record + resolver that reads staged trust-root only when a separate, later-dated activation receipt selects it), so the merge that introduces the change is provably distinct from the change that makes it effective.
findings.acceptance_test: Merge a trust-root edit and show, via the resolver/effective-state, that the old rule is still in force until a separate activation record is committed; then commit the activation record and show the new rule becomes effective. Prove the two commits are authored by distinct authorization events.

findings.claim: No enforced 'Class B / ordinary self-development' classification exists for self-development changes; the repo's 'Class B' vocabulary refers exclusively to evidence-retention pointer artifacts, and risk-materiality tiers key on action type (mutate_repo / protected_branch_mutation), not on whether a change touches the trust root.
findings.consequence: FD-017 distinguishes 'ordinary self-dev follows Class B' from 'trust-root changes'. In this repo, 'Class B' means Git-pointer evidence manifests (retention/README.md:32, state/evidence/README.md:35) — unrelated to a self-development risk class. risk-materiality.yml classifies by action_type; a trust-root edit and a docs edit both map to `mutate_repo` (moderate/ACP-2) unless they touch a protected branch. The octon-self-evolution program.yml prohibits `autonomous_constitutional_amendment` and `self_modifying_runtime` (program.yml:20-25), which is the closest expression of the FD-017 trust-root/ordinary split, but it is a governance YAML that no merge gate reads and the program itself is never invoked (see F-017-1). So the taxonomy that FD-017 assumes (an ordinary-self-dev class vs a trust-root class with different, enforced controls) is not materialized as an enforceable classifier.
findings.minimum_repair: Add an authoritative trust-root inventory + a self-development change classifier (policy + validator) that maps a diff's touched paths to {ordinary-self-dev, trust-root} and binds each class to distinct required evidence/gates; reference program.yml prohibited_change_classes from the enforced gate so the class boundary is machine-checked, not prose.
findings.acceptance_test: Run the new classifier against a diff touching only docs (expect: ordinary-self-dev, base gate set) and a diff touching .octon/framework/constitution/** or a gate workflow (expect: trust-root, elevated gate set incl. independent verifier + activation). Confirm both are wired as required checks.

findings.claim: Harness self-activation has no operator-preauthorized, previous-version-verified, exact-version, staged, rollback-capable process; the runtime binary is built and shipped from HEAD via unsigned artifacts, with no gate where the prior harness version verifies the new one and no immutable verifier the candidate cannot edit.
findings.consequence: runtime-binaries.yml builds `octon_kernel` release binaries from the tagged HEAD and publishes them via softprops/action-gh-release (runtime-binaries.yml:122-182) with no signing/cosign/sigstore/GPG step (grep for sign/cosign/sigstore/gpg over workflows+spec returned only attestation-envelope schema fields and an unrelated auditor_signoff enum). release-please.yml (unsigned, PAT-driven) creates the tag. There is no gate in which the *previous* installed harness version verifies the *new* candidate, no exact-version pin binding a verifier that the candidate cannot change, and no staged rollout/rollback-capable activation of the harness itself — the release runbook (release-runbook.md:32-61) is a manual checklist. Combined with F-017-2 (verifiers run from the change's own head), an autonomous agent could ship a new harness that alters its own activation and verification rules. FD-018's five conjuncts (operator-preauthorized, previous-version-verified, exact-version, staged, rollback-capable, rules-immutable-to-candidate) are essentially ABSENT / at best REQUIRES_FRESH_PROVIDER_EVIDENCE for the operator-preauthorization piece.
findings.minimum_repair: Sign release artifacts and pin an exact previous-version verifier (a released, tagged binary or an out-of-tree signed verifier) that must validate the new candidate before activation; require an operator-preauthorized activation approval keyed to the exact new version; make harness activation staged (canary/soak per governance-model.md) with a retained rollback handle; ensure the verification/activation/rollback rules live outside the candidate's own change surface (base-ref or signed external ref).
findings.acceptance_test: Attempt to publish a runtime binary whose source alters the activation gate: activation must be blocked until (a) the signed previous-version verifier validates the exact new version, (b) an operator preauthorization for that version exists, and (c) a rollback handle is retained. Confirm the verifier/activation rules cannot be satisfied by files edited in the same release change.

findings.claim: The declarative promotion/amendment/decision-request contracts do assert the correct non-self-authorization posture (decision_request_authorizes_promotion:false, promotion_runtime_self_approves:false, human_or_quorum_approval_required:true, recertification failure_blocks_closure:true), but every one of these checks is embedded in the same editable governance surface and enforced only by the un-wired evolution CLI, so the strong-looking contract is not on an unavoidable enforced boundary.
findings.consequence: promotion_blockers() (evolution.rs:541-787) is a genuinely thorough fail-closed reader: it requires accepted decision refs, human/quorum approval, lab gate pass, rollback posture, recertification request/result, support-no-widening proof, and rejects self-approval (promotion_runtime_self_approves must be false; decision_request_authorizes_promotion is const false in the schema). These are strong primitives worth preserving. BUT the caller `apply_promotion` never mutates anything and no gate calls it (F-017-1), and the policy/schema files that define the boundary are themselves editable trust-root files certified by their own head-ref run (F-017-2). Net: the mediation asserted by these contracts is advisory. This mirrors the pre-existing 'Octon mediation gap' (engine enforces in-kernel but nothing unavoidable calls it for agent effects).
findings.minimum_repair: Route the actual landing of a trust-root/self-evolution change through `promotion_blockers`/`octon promote apply` as a required, base-ref-run gate (see F-017-1/F-017-2), so the already-correct non-self-authorization logic becomes an unavoidable boundary rather than an optional CLI report.
findings.acceptance_test: With the gate wired and run from a trusted ref, feed a promotion record whose `promotion_runtime_self_approves:true` or whose decision ref is missing/ungranted; the gate must block the merge. Flip to a valid, granted, human-approved record and confirm it passes.

decision_alignment.rationale: The INTENT of FD-017 is well-expressed in governance prose and in strong declarative contracts: octon-self-evolution program.yml prohibits autonomous_constitutional_amendment and self_modifying_runtime; the self-evolution-decision-request schema hard-codes decision_request_authorizes_promotion:false and decision_request_authorizes_material_execution:false; promotion-runtime-v1.md states 'Promotion Runtime does not approve its own promotion'; promotion_blockers() in evolution.rs is a genuinely thorough fail-closed reader that rejects self-approval and requires human/quorum approval. HOWEVER the enforcement is not real: (1) the evolution/promotion/recertification runtime is CLI inspection-only and is wired into NO merge gate (F-017-1); (2) the CI gates that do run on authority/trust-root diffs check out and execute the PR's OWN head ref, so a change can weaken or delete its own gate/validator/policy and be certified by the edited version — same-change self-certification (F-017-2); (3) there is NO inert-landing mechanism — authored authority under framework/** and instance/** (constitution, charter, policies, workflows, validators) is effective the instant it merges (F-017-3); (4) the 'ordinary self-dev = Class B' vs 'trust-root' split FD-017 relies on is not materialized as an enforced classifier ('Class B' in-repo means evidence-retention pointers), and no trust-root inventory exists (F-017-4). So the 'cannot self-certify' and 'land inert' clauses are ABSENT as controls; the non-self-authorization posture is SATISFIED only at the declarative/advisory layer.

FD-018 requires that autonomous trust-root activation happen ONLY inside a process that is operator-preauthorized, previous-version-verified, exact-version, staged, rollback-capable, and whose own rules the candidate cannot change. None of these conjuncts is implemented for harness self-activation: (1) no operator-preauthorization gate keyed to a specific new version exists on the effective path; (2) there is NO previous-version-verifies-new-version step — release binaries are built from HEAD in runtime-binaries.yml with no prior-version verifier; (3) no exact-version pin binds an immutable verifier; (4) release artifacts are UNSIGNED (no cosign/sigstore/gpg anywhere in workflows/spec) and shipped via action-gh-release; (5) there is no staged/canary activation of the harness itself and no retained rollback handle for a harness version — the release runbook is a manual checklist; (6) crucially, the candidate CAN change its own verification/activation/rollback rules because workflow files, validator scripts, and policy YAML are all editable in the same change and are executed live/from-head (F-017-2, F-018-1). The only 'activation' concept in the repo governs the live *disclosure/release* claim as documentation discipline, not a runtime-enforced, candidate-immutable harness activation. The operator-preauthorization dimension could be argued to sit partly in GitHub branch rulesets / AUTONOMY_PAT, which is provider-side and REQUIRES_FRESH_PROVIDER_EVIDENCE, but even granting that, the previous-version-verified / exact-version / staged / rules-immutable conjuncts are absent.

strengths_to_preserve: promotion_blockers() in .octon/framework/engine/runtime/crates/kernel/src/commands/evolution.rs:541-787 is a thorough fail-closed reader: it rejects promotion_runtime_self_approves != false, requires accepted/granted decision refs (validate_approval_or_decision_ref:852-903 checks status=granted, workflow_mode role-mediated/human-only, quorum policy), requires lab-gate pass, rollback posture, recertification request+result, support-no-widening proof, durable decision refs, and generated-refresh refs. This is the right enforcement logic — it just needs to be placed on an unavoidable, base-ref-run boundary.

The self-evolution-decision-request-v1 schema hard-codes decision_request_authorizes_promotion:const false and decision_request_authorizes_material_execution:const false (spec/self-evolution-decision-request-v1.schema.json:43-44), and recertification-result-v1 hard-codes failure_blocks_closure:const true (recertification-result-v1.schema.json:52). These const constraints correctly encode non-self-authorization and fail-closed-on-recertification.

octon-self-evolution program.yml prohibited_change_classes explicitly names autonomous_constitutional_amendment, autonomous_support_target_widening, ai_only_quorum, and self_modifying_runtime (program.yml:20-25) and sets required_approval_posture: human_or_quorum_required and program_mutates_authority_directly:false — a clear, correct statement of the FD-017/FD-018 boundary that just needs machine enforcement.

constitutional-amendment-policy.yml enumerates constitutional_kernel, authority_hierarchy, execution_authorization_boundary, fail_closed_posture, and self_evolution_approval_rules as amendment-gated surfaces (constitutional-amendment-policy.yml:5-16) — this is effectively a partial trust-root inventory that could seed the missing enforced classifier.

The trust CLI (trust.rs) consistently stamps *_authorizes_execution:false, external_registry_is_authority:false, and fail-closed routing on every trust/attestation/proof/lease/compact record, keeping external trust artifacts as evidence-only and never authority — a good non-widening posture to preserve for the trust-root perimeter.

main-change-route-guard.yml already has a break-glass ledger-linkage enforcement for charter edits (lines 471-516) requiring an OVR override record with break_glass:true and running governance lint/audit — a usable seed for an independent, base-ref-anchored trust-root gate.
uncertainties: Operator-preauthorization for activation may be partly encoded in GitHub branch rulesets and the AUTONOMY_PAT secret (provider-side), which I cannot inspect statically (read-only, no live provider access). Whether the live main ruleset requires human review for trust-root paths is REQUIRES_FRESH_PROVIDER_EVIDENCE. github-control-plane-contract.json declares require_review_thread_resolution:false for universal main rules and protected_main_bypass_allowed:false, but the actual live ruleset is authoritative and was not observed.

I did not fully read validate-authorization-boundary-coverage.sh or assert-protected-execution-posture.sh; it is possible one of them contains a trust-root-specific check I did not see. My conclusion that no gate wires the evolution/promotion runtime is based on grepping .github/workflows for evolve/promote/recertif (only uec-cutover-certify matched) and reading the closure/deny-by-default/self-containment gate step lists — but a validator script could invoke the kernel indirectly; this was not exhaustively traced.

Whether any external/out-of-tree process (not in this repo) performs previous-version verification or signing of released binaries is unknown; I only inspected in-repo workflows and specs. If such a process exists it is DEPLOYMENT_LOCAL and not evidenced here.

The `octon promote apply` runtime states 'requires_authorized_run_for_material_change' — I did not locate the concrete 'authorized governed run' code path that would perform the actual material write for a promotion (apply_promotion itself writes nothing). It is unclear whether such a material-write path exists anywhere in the runtime or whether promotions are expected to be applied purely by ordinary git edits, which would make the promotion runtime entirely advisory.

results.subagent: Subagent G — Workspace Projects, Profiles, Harness Factory, Extensions (FD-019, FD-020, FD-021, FD-023)

findings.claim: No durable, digest-bound 'Workspace Project' identity exists in current authored/framework/generated surfaces; only a singleton mutable Project Profile (`instance/locality/project-profile.yml`) exists, and the base + constitutional profile schemas set `additionalProperties: true` with NO registry/lifecycle/dependency/revision-pointer/authority contract. The 'Workspace Project' concept appears only inside an unaccepted exploratory proposal tree.
findings.consequence: FD-019's 'durable Workspace Project identity referencing Project Profiles' is not realized. The current identity is a single machine-path-bound Profile with no multi-project identity, no immutable-revision store, and no digest-bound maximum-boundary pointer. There is no durable, authenticated project boundary that policy/authority could independently verify as a maximum locality ceiling; the only boundary primitives are the descriptive `protected_zones`/`governance_relevant_paths` arrays in the profile and the `octon-locality-scope-v2` scope (single `octon-harness` scope).
findings.minimum_repair: Introduce a minimal `workspace-project-v1` identity contract (schema_version, project_id, repo/ownership identity, maximum locality boundary, dependency refs, and a `profile_revision_ref` pointer to the refreshable Project Profile) plus a project registry under `instance/locality/`, explicitly classified non-authoritative, and wire it as a read input to policy/authority without granting effects. Keep the existing Profile as the refreshable descriptive half.
findings.acceptance_test: grep confirms a `workspace-project-v1` (or equivalent) schema and a durable project-identity record outside `inputs/exploratory/**`; the record carries a digest/revision pointer to `project-profile.yml`; a schema/validator asserts it declares no route/effect/grant fields; and a validator run treats it as a non-authorizing read input.

findings.claim: The existing Project Profile satisfies FD-019's 'never authority' clause: the `project-profile-v1` schema exposes only descriptive discovery fields (repo_structure, toolchain discovery, hints, protected_zones, governance_relevant_paths, validation_strategy, rollback_constraints) and NO route/effect/grant/scope-minting keys; the product feature note explicitly states the compiler 'does not mint runtime authority', and the kernel treats it as an evidence-compiled read artifact with a `ProjectProfileStaleness` (refreshability) signal.
findings.consequence: The 'never authority' half of FD-019 is well anchored today; the descriptive Profile cannot grant effects. The risk is only structural: `additionalProperties: true` on both profile schemas means a widened profile could smuggle non-schema keys, but nothing in the runtime consumes profile fields as authority, so this is latent rather than active.
findings.minimum_repair: When adding Workspace Project identity, tighten `additionalProperties` to false (or an explicit allowlist) on the identity/boundary contract so a self-widened profile/project record cannot introduce authority-shaped fields; retain the descriptive profile as-is.
findings.acceptance_test: A schema-conformance validator rejects any project/profile record containing route/effect/grant/capability keys; adding such a key to `project-profile.yml` fails validation.

findings.claim: A deterministic Harness Factory exists and is digest-bound: `generate-runtime-effective-route-bundle.sh` hashes a fixed set of approved effective inputs (root manifest, runtime-resolution, support matrix, pack routes + lock, extension catalog + generation lock, workflow manifest) into `route-bundle.yml` + `route-bundle.lock.yml`, records `source_digests`, `freshness.mode: digest_bound`, `invalidation_conditions`, `non_authority_classification: derived-runtime-handle`, and forbidden consumers; the generator is idempotent (reuse-if-payload-unchanged).
findings.consequence: FD-020's 'deterministic Harness Factory compiles approved inputs into a digest-bound effective manifest' is realized. The bundle compiles routes/tuples and does not itself decide/schedule; it emits `allow`/`stage_only`/`requires_mission` from precompiled tiers, matching 'not another runtime/scheduler/policy engine'.
findings.minimum_repair: None required for satisfaction. Optional hardening: pin the input set in a machine-readable factory input manifest so an added authority input cannot silently enter the digest set.
findings.acceptance_test: Re-running the generator on an unchanged input set is a no-op (idempotent); mutating any declared source input changes the bundle/lock digests and receipt; a stale bundle is rejected downstream (see G-04).

findings.claim: Stale or self-widened effective manifests cannot launch: the `runtime_resolver` crate enforces the digest binding IN-KERNEL. `verify_runtime_route_bundle` denies on generation_id mismatch, `route_bundle_sha256` drift, runtime-resolution digest drift, root-manifest/support-matrix digest mismatch, receipt digest/generation/status/published-path mismatch, and requires dependency handles for v3; `handles.rs` performs per-dependency `verify_digest_field`/`enforce_freshness_mode`/`allows_consumer`, emitting `CAPABILITY_DENIED` on drift. The freshness-gates-v4 spec codifies 'stale or missing runtime-effective handle: deny' and 'pack widening beyond admitted tuple: deny'.
findings.consequence: The 'can a stale or self-widened manifest launch?' probe is answered NO by static inspection of the resolver: the effective manifest is a derived non-authority handle whose trust collapses on any input drift, and the resolver refuses drifted/forbidden-consumer handles. This is a strength: the Harness Factory output is compile-time-fixed and runtime-verified, not a live authority surface.
findings.minimum_repair: None for FD-020. Residual: I did not DYNAMICALLY_EXECUTE the resolver; a runtime proof (deliberately drift a digest and observe CAPABILITY_DENIED) would upgrade this from architectural inference of the deny path to executed proof.
findings.acceptance_test: REQUIRES_DYNAMIC_PROOF: mutate `route-bundle.yml` (or an upstream source input) without regenerating the lock, run the resolver, and confirm it returns CAPABILITY_DENIED (digest drift) rather than launching.

findings.claim: A private signed extension catalog with import/verify/pin/quarantine exists: normalized packs live under `inputs/additive/extensions/<pack-id>/` (import via governed intake), `pack.yml` is `octon-extension-pack-v5` carrying `provenance{source_id,imported_from,origin_uri,digest_sha256,attestation_refs}` and trust classes (first_party_bundled=allow, first_party_external=require_acknowledgement, third_party=deny); publication produces a digest-pinned effective catalog + generation lock + artifact map with `invalidation_conditions` and receipt SHAs; invalid/denied packs quarantine under `state/control/extensions/quarantine.yml`; publication status supports `published | published_with_quarantine | withdrawn`. There is NO public marketplace surface.
findings.consequence: FD-021's import/verify/pin plus revoke-by-quarantine/withdraw and the 'no public marketplace' constraint are realized. This is a genuine strength: trust is repo-owned in `instance/extensions.yml`, provenance travels with the pack, and runtime consumes only the digest-pinned published view.
findings.minimum_repair: None for the import/verify/pin/quarantine/no-marketplace clauses.
findings.acceptance_test: grep confirms no marketplace endpoint/URL surface; `validate-extension-publication-state.sh` enforces quarantine/status invariants; the generation lock pins desired-config + root-manifest SHAs; a denied `third_party` pack is quarantined and excluded from the effective catalog.

findings.claim: Two clauses of FD-021 are only partially met: (a) 'signed' — the schema supports `digest_sha256` + `attestation_refs`, but every currently-shipped pack is `first_party_bundled` with `digest_sha256: null` and `attestation_refs: []`, and signature/attestation is required only for `first_party_external`/`third_party`, so no signature is actually enforced on the live catalog; (b) 'rollback' — publication models revoke via `withdrawn` and re-publish-from-config, but there is no first-class 'roll back the extension catalog to a prior published generation/pin' operation distinct from regenerating from the current desired config.
findings.consequence: The catalog is 'signable' but not 'signed' in practice, and 'rollback' is emergent (re-publish/withdraw) rather than a named pin-restore. FD-021 as written ('import/verify/pin/revoke/rollback' + 'signed') is therefore satisfied in spirit but has two thin spots: unenforced signatures on the shipped set and no explicit rollback-to-prior-generation primitive.
findings.minimum_repair: (a) Populate `digest_sha256` for bundled packs and add a validator assertion that every published pack carries a non-null content digest (even bundled), so the catalog is content-signed end to end; (b) add an explicit `rollback_to_generation`/prior-lock-restore operation (or document that withdraw+republish-from-pinned-config is the sanctioned rollback and gate it on a retained prior generation lock).
findings.acceptance_test: A validator fails if any published pack has `digest_sha256: null`; and an operator can restore the effective catalog to a named prior `generation_id` with a receipt, or the governance docs explicitly define the withdraw+republish rollback path with a retained prior lock.

findings.claim: Extensions/projects/harnesses cannot mint or widen authority: the extension boundary contract forbids governance/authority/orchestration/engine/assurance/services content in raw packs and restricts runtime consumption to the generated effective view; model/host adapters (the provider-native delegation surface) are `authority_mode: non_authoritative`/`projection_only`, `replaceable: const true`, and carry explicit `non_authoritative_boundaries` ('may not widen authority or support tiers'); the route bundle is `derived-runtime-handle` non-authority; the freshness spec denies 'pack widening beyond admitted tuple'.
findings.consequence: The 'they must not mint or widen authority' constraint spanning FD-019/020/021/023 is structurally enforced: none of these surfaces is an authority class, and both the effective manifest and adapters classify themselves as non-authority. This is a core strength to preserve.
findings.minimum_repair: None. Optional: add an assurance check asserting adapter manifests keep `authority_mode` in the non-authoritative enum and `non_authoritative_boundaries` non-empty, so a future adapter cannot silently omit the boundary.
findings.acceptance_test: A validator fails any adapter manifest with an authority-granting mode or empty `non_authoritative_boundaries`; the boundary-contract validator rejects governance/engine/authority content in a raw pack.

findings.claim: Provider-native component delegation with Octon-owned semantics and trust contracts is realized via the constitutional adapter contract family. `model-adapter-v1` defines `integration_class: provider-bridge | native-planning | local-model` and mandates Octon-owned trust surfaces: `conformance_criteria_refs`, `conformance_suite_refs`, `contamination_reset_policy`, `memory_discipline_policy`, `support_target_ref` subordination, `known_limitations`, and `non_authoritative_boundaries`. The live `frontier-governed` adapter uses `integration_class: provider-bridge` and binds `interface_ref` to Octon's `policy-interface-v1`, i.e., the provider plugs into an Octon-owned interface and Octon owns the semantics/trust.
findings.consequence: FD-023 is realized: provider-native model/host components are delegated to through replaceable, non-authoritative Octon-owned adapter contracts; Octon owns the interface (policy-interface-v1), the conformance/trust obligations, and the support-target ceiling. Provider behavior 'may shape execution quality but may not widen authority or support tiers.'
findings.minimum_repair: None for satisfaction. Note: connector-level provider delegation (connector-trust-dossier, connector-admission, tool-connector-posture) exists as a broader contract family but I inspected the model/host adapters primarily; a connector-side confirmation would broaden coverage.
findings.acceptance_test: A schema-conformance validator confirms every model/host adapter manifest declares `authority_mode` non-authoritative, `replaceable: true`, a bound Octon `interface_ref`, and non-empty conformance + non_authoritative_boundaries; a provider-bridge adapter cannot declare support tiers beyond `support-targets.yml`.

decision_alignment.rationale: The 'refreshable Project Profile, never authority' half is realized: a singleton `instance/locality/project-profile.yml` (project-profile-v1) carries identity fields (profile_id, repo_root, profile_scope, status) plus workspace-charter refs and evidence/source-fact roots, is compiled from source-facts by the kernel engagement command, has a ProjectProfileStaleness refresh signal, and exposes only descriptive discovery/hint/protected-zone fields with NO authority-minting keys (product note: 'does not mint runtime authority'). BUT the 'minimal inferred durable Workspace Project identity referencing Project Profiles' half is ABSENT from current authored/framework/generated surfaces: both profile schemas set additionalProperties:true with no project registry/lifecycle/dependency/revision-pointer/maximum-boundary contract, and the 'Workspace Project' concept appears only inside the unaccepted exploratory proposal `octon-trustworthy-autonomy-solo-developer-revision-2` (which itself records the current gap as P-07 'singleton mutable Project Profile carries a machine path but not durable multi-project identity'). So durable Workspace Project identity is proposal-only.

A deterministic, digest-bound Harness Factory exists and is enforced end to end. `generate-runtime-effective-route-bundle.sh` hashes a fixed approved input set into `route-bundle.yml` + `route-bundle.lock.yml` with source_digests, freshness.mode digest_bound, invalidation_conditions, dependency handles, receipt linkage, and idempotent reuse; the output is classified `derived-runtime-handle` non-authority with explicit forbidden_consumers. The `runtime_resolver` crate enforces this in-kernel: `verify_runtime_route_bundle` and `handles.rs` deny (CAPABILITY_DENIED) on generation-id mismatch, route/source/root-manifest/support-matrix digest drift, receipt drift, forbidden consumer, or missing dependency handles, and freshness-gates-v4 codifies 'stale handle: deny' and 'pack widening beyond admitted tuple: deny'. The factory only compiles precomputed tiers into routes; it does not schedule/decide/police, matching 'not another runtime/scheduler/policy engine'. A stale or self-widened manifest cannot launch by static inspection.

A private, digest-pinned extension catalog with import (governed intake -> normalized packs under inputs/additive/extensions), verify (compatibility + provenance trust classes: first_party_bundled=allow, first_party_external=require_acknowledgement, third_party=deny), pin (generation lock pinning desired-config + root-manifest + receipt SHAs, plus invalidation_conditions), and revoke (quarantine.yml, publication statuses published/published_with_quarantine/withdrawn) is implemented, with runtime consuming only the published effective view and NO public marketplace surface. Two clauses are only partial: (1) 'signed' is a schema capability (provenance.digest_sha256 + attestation_refs) but is unenforced on the shipped set — every live pack is first_party_bundled with digest_sha256:null and attestation_refs:[], and signatures are required only for external/third-party classes; (2) 'rollback' is emergent (withdraw + re-publish-from-config) rather than a named restore-to-prior-generation primitive.

Provider-native component delegation with Octon-owned semantics and trust contracts is realized through the constitutional adapter contract family. `model-adapter-v1` defines integration_class provider-bridge/native-planning/local-model and mandates Octon-owned trust surfaces (conformance_criteria_refs, conformance_suite_refs, contamination_reset_policy, memory_discipline, support_target subordination, non_authoritative_boundaries) with replaceable:const true and authority_mode enum non_authoritative; host-adapter-v1 is analogous (projection_only/non_authoritative). The live frontier-governed adapter uses integration_class:provider-bridge and binds interface_ref to Octon's policy-interface-v1, and both live adapters declare 'provider-specific behavior may shape execution quality but may not widen authority or support tiers.' Octon owns the interface, conformance obligations, and support ceiling; providers plug in as replaceable non-authority bridges.

strengths_to_preserve: Runtime-enforced digest-bound Harness Factory: runtime_resolver::verify_runtime_route_bundle + handles.rs verify_digest_field/enforce_freshness_mode make the effective route bundle a derived non-authority handle whose trust collapses on any input drift (CAPABILITY_DENIED). This is the enforcement backbone for FD-020.

Publication-freshness-gates-v4 spec (.octon/framework/engine/runtime/spec/publication-freshness-gates-v4.md): a clear, testable deny-list (stale handle, receipt drift, raw-path bypass, quarantined extension in route, pack widening beyond admitted tuple) that all generated/effective consumers are held to.

Extension trust model: repo-owned trust in instance/extensions.yml (allow/require_acknowledgement/deny by origin class), provenance travelling with pack.yml, quarantine.yml, and three publication statuses (published/published_with_quarantine/withdrawn) — a real revoke path without a public marketplace.

Constitutional adapter contract family (adapters/*.schema.json): model/host adapters are replaceable:const true, authority_mode non_authoritative, with mandatory non_authoritative_boundaries, conformance refs, contamination_reset_policy, and support_target subordination — a clean provider-native delegation surface that cannot widen authority (FD-023).

Extension boundary-contract.md: raw packs are barred from carrying governance/authority/orchestration/engine/assurance content and runtime must consume only the generated effective view — prevents extensions becoming a second authority surface.

Project Profile as pure descriptive discovery artifact: project-profile-v1 has no effect/route/grant keys and the compiler explicitly 'does not mint runtime authority', preserving the 'never authority' invariant for FD-019's existing half.
uncertainties: I did not DYNAMICALLY_EXECUTE the runtime_resolver; the 'stale/self-widened manifest cannot launch' conclusion for FD-020 is ARCHITECTURAL_INFERENCE from reading the deny paths in lib.rs/handles.rs, not an executed proof. A dynamic drift-and-observe test (mutate a source digest, run resolver, expect CAPABILITY_DENIED) would confirm.

For FD-021 'signed', I confirmed digest_sha256:null and attestation_refs:[] only on the packs I read (nextjs, octon-concept-integration); I did not enumerate every pack.yml, so the signature-enforcement gap is medium-confidence for the whole set rather than exhaustively proven.

I did not fully trace the extension publication generator implementation (validate-extension-publication-state.sh is 48k; I read the status-handling and quarantine sections). Whether a first-class rollback-to-prior-generation operation exists elsewhere (e.g., a generator script or kernel command) beyond withdraw/re-publish is not fully excluded.

For FD-019, I treated the 'Workspace Project' proposal tree under inputs/exploratory as unaccepted per instructions and did not rely on its claims as proof; I independently verified the current-state gap from the schemas and instance/locality contents. If a Workspace Project identity contract exists under a name I did not grep (no hits for workspace_project/WorkspaceProject/durable-project-identity outside the proposal), it would change the FD-019 alignment.

FD-023 coverage focused on model/host adapters; the broader connector contract family (connector-trust-dossier, connector-admission, tool-connector-posture) also implements provider delegation and trust dossiers but was not deeply read, so connector-side FD-023 details are less certain than the model/host adapter conclusion.

results.subagent: Subagent H — Product Scope, Usability, Simplification (FD-001, FD-002, FD-024)

findings.claim: The repo's 'Class A/B/C' taxonomy is an EVIDENCE-RETENTION storage class (Git-inline / Git-pointer / external-digest), NOT the FD-002 consequence-class routing (autonomous / brokered+auto-completed / stronger-controls). The actual consequence/autonomy routing uses a DIFFERENT and much richer taxonomy: mission_class (observe/campaign/reconcile/maintenance/migration/incident/destructive) crossed with risk tiers ACP-0..ACP-4, materiality classes, reversibility classes, and machine quorum requirements. There is no code or contract that names 'Class A/B/C' as the run-routing axis FD-002 describes.
findings.consequence: FD-002's promised simple three-bucket model ('concentrates ceremony at actual consequence boundaries') is not what the code implements. The implemented model is a 7x5 mission-class x ACP-tier matrix with quorum, burn states, circuit breakers, and safing subsets — far more surface than 'Class A autonomous / Class B brokered / Class C stronger controls'. A reviewer testing FD-002 by grepping for Class A/B/C routing will find only the unrelated retention taxonomy, and the naming collision (same words, different meaning) is itself a discoverability/usability hazard for a solo operator.
findings.minimum_repair: Either (a) add an explicit crosswalk contract mapping the FD-002 Class A=autonomous / Class B=brokered+auto-completed / Class C=stronger-controls buckets onto the existing mission_class + ACP-tier + reversibility model, or (b) collapse the implemented matrix toward the three named buckets.
